Imagine a person who almost never smiles. They speak in a flat, heavy tone. Their face looks like it has been set in stone — hard, tight, and cold. Being around them feels like standing under a grey, overcast sky. That person is dour.

Dour describes someone (or something) that is stern, gloomy, and completely without warmth or humor. It is not just a bad mood — it is more like a permanent personality. A dour person carries a sense of harshness and joylessness about them at all times.

The word carries three qualities that usually work together:

1. Sternness
A dour person is strict, hard, and unyielding. They are not warm or approachable. They set firm rules and expectations, and they do not bend easily. Think of a headmaster who treats every small mistake as a serious crime.

2. Gloominess
A dour person has a persistently dark and pessimistic outlook. They seem to expect things to go wrong. There is a heavy, cheerless weight that follows them everywhere. They are not dramatic about it — they just quietly carry this cloud around them.

3. Humorlessness
This is important. A dour person does not laugh. They do not joke. If you try to be funny around them, your humor dies in the air. It is not that they are offended — it is more that joy and lightness simply do not reach them.
Sharpening the Meaning — What "Dour" Is Not

Because dour is close to several other words, it helps to know where it stands apart:

  • Dour ≠ Sad. A sad person is hurting and emotional. A dour person is not necessarily suffering — they are simply locked, cold, and hard. Sadness is soft; dour is rigid.
  • Dour ≠ Angry. An angry person is fired up. A dour person is not explosive — they are more like a heavy, immovable rock. Anger is hot; dour is cold.
  • Dour ≠ Shy or Quiet. A shy person holds back because they are nervous. A dour person holds back because warmth simply is not part of who they are.
  • Dour ≠ Serious. This is the trickiest one. A serious person can still smile, care deeply, and make others feel welcome. A dour person takes seriousness to such an extreme that it becomes off-putting and joyless. Think of "serious" as a dial — dour is when you turn it up all the way until the warmth completely disappears.

These sentences will show you how the word behaves in real use:

  • "The dour teacher never smiled, even when the whole class burst out laughing."

Here, dour tells us the teacher's expression and personality are hard and cheerless.

  • "He gave a dour nod and walked away without saying a word."

The nod itself communicates the character — stiff, cold, unwelcoming.

  • "She had a dour outlook on life — she always assumed that something would go wrong."

Here, dour describes a way of thinking and seeing the world.

  • "The old guard sat in dour silence while everyone else celebrated."

The silence here is not just quiet — it is heavy, disapproving, and joyless.

  • "The countryside in deep winter had a dour beauty — grey skies, bare trees, and empty roads."

Notice that dour can also describe places and atmospheres, not just people. A dour landscape is one that feels bleak, harsh, and unwelcoming.
How to Recognise a "Dour" Person or Thing

Ask yourself these quick questions:

  • Does this person (or place, or atmosphere) feel joyless and heavy?
  • Does warmth seem to bounce off them without landing?
  • Do they seem permanently set in a state of grimness — not from a single bad day, but as a feature of who they are?
  • Is there a sense of hardness and severity that makes you slightly hesitant to approach?

If yes to most of these, dour is the right word.

One last thing worth noting: dour is not a dramatic word. It does not shout. In fact, it perfectly matches what it describes — it is a blunt, heavy, quiet sort of word. When you use it, you are not describing someone who is falling apart or causing a scene. You are describing a quiet, settled, unyielding grimness — and that is exactly what makes it such a precise and powerful word.
